what: Triple Flag Precious Metals owns streams and royalties on mines. It pays a mining company cash upfront in exchange for the right to buy a share of future gold or silver production at a fixed low price, or for a percentage of the mine’s revenue, and then collects for the life of the asset without paying operating costs.
customers: It has no customers in the ordinary sense. Its counterparties are mining companies seeking finance, and its income comes from selling gold and silver at market prices.
money: Gold received or royalties collected from producing mines.
Silver streams and royalties on other metals.
moat: A stream holder captures the benefit of higher metal prices and of the operator finding more ore, without paying for cost inflation, equipment failures, labour disputes or capital overruns. Royalties and streams last the life of the mine and often cover ground not yet explored, so the asset can grow without the owner spending a further dollar.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $66.7M, because buying new streams shows as an investing outflow before any income arrives.
The shares trade at about 11.4 times sales and 15.3 times EV/EBITDA, a premium that reflects the quality of the model rather than cheapness.
Income is concentrated in a modest number of mines, so an operational problem at a significant one matters.
Overpaying for a stream is the only real way to destroy value here, and competition for good assets is intense.
Only four analysts cover the stock, so the $39.25 average target rests on very thin coverage.
opportunities: A net margin of 61.7% shows the model plainly: almost nothing sits between revenue and profit.
Revenue has grown very fast, from $150.4M in 2021 to $388.7M in 2025, with trailing revenue of $501.8M.
No debt reported, and $88.7M of cash, so none of the balance sheet risk that periodically destroys miners.
Gold price increases flow almost directly to profit because the cost base barely moves.
Exploration success at the operator’s expense expands the asset at no cost to the stream holder.
watch: New stream and royalty acquisitions and the price paid. Existing streams require no management; value is created or destroyed entirely in what gets bought.
view: Streaming and royalty companies are the best way to own metal prices, and the reason is an asymmetry that does not exist anywhere else in mining. The operator bears rising labour costs, equipment breakdowns, permitting delays, environmental liabilities and capital overruns, and keeps whatever remains. The stream holder receives its share of the production or revenue and pays for none of it. When gold rises, the stream holder captures it fully while the miner’s costs rise too. When the operator spends to extend the mine’s life, the stream covers the new ounces for free.

A 61.7% net margin is that structure showing up in the accounts. There is almost nothing between revenue and profit because there is almost nothing to pay for — no mines, no equipment, no workforce. It is also why these companies trade at multiples that look absurd next to miners, and why comparing them to miners is a category error. The right comparison is to other royalty companies.

Triple Flag’s growth has been genuinely impressive — $150 million to $389 million of revenue in four years, now $502 million trailing — helped by a rising gold price doing exactly what the model promises. The balance sheet carries no debt, which removes the one thing that has repeatedly destroyed mining companies. Four analysts covering a $5.7 billion company means this is under-examined, which cuts both ways.

The only genuine management decision in this business is what to buy and what to pay, and that is where I would focus entirely. Existing streams pay automatically and need nobody. Competition for good new streams is fierce — Franco-Nevada and Wheaton have cheaper capital and more scale — which pushes smaller buyers toward paying more or accepting lower-quality assets. The negative free cash flow is not a warning here; it is the company buying future income. Whether it bought well will not be visible for years, so the acquisition record over a full cycle, rather than this year’s revenue, is what should drive a view.
bull: Gold prices hold while operators expand reserves underneath existing streams at no cost, and new streams are acquired at prices that earn their keep.
bear: Concentration in a handful of mines meets an operational problem, or competition for streams pushes management into overpaying for weaker assets.
